stimulus.text: Original secondary passage: When World War II ended, sixteen million American veterans came home to a country that had to shift from making weapons to making peacetime goods. Factories laid off workers, prices rose, and returning soldiers crowded the job market. Congress had already passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill, offering veterans low-interest loans for homes and money for college. At the same time, birthrates rose sharply as veterans married and started families.

stem: The GI Bill is often remembered as a program that built the postwar middle class. Which of the following best explains why that memory is incomplete?

options.text: Black veterans were largely shut out, so the middle class it built was mostly white.
The bill helped only officers, while ordinary soldiers received nothing at all.
options.misconception: Millions of ordinary soldiers used the GI Bill for school and homes; it was not officers only.

options.text: The bill was never actually passed by Congress, so no veteran ever used it.
options.misconception: The GI Bill was real law, passed in 1944, and millions of veterans used its benefits.

options.text: The bill's benefits went mostly to women who had never served in the armed forces.
options.misconception: GI Bill benefits went to people who had served in the armed forces, not to civilians.

rationales.A: The GI Bill's benefits were real, but they were not shared equally. Background from the books: southern states set high barriers for Black veterans, and in Mississippi in 1947 only two of 3,200 home loans went to Black veterans.
rationales.B: Ordinary soldiers used the bill in large numbers. Background from the books: nearly eight million veterans used its education benefits by 1956.
rationales.C: Congress did pass the bill, as the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, and millions of veterans used it.
rationales.D: The bill's benefits went to veterans, men and women who had served. Women who had never served did not receive them.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the proud story. The GI Bill sent millions of veterans to college and into new homes.
2. Ask who was left out. Background from the books: states set the rules for benefits, and southern states set high barriers for Black veterans.
3. Look at the numbers. Background from the books: in Mississippi in 1947, only two of 3,200 home loans backed by the Veterans Administration went to Black veterans.
4. Name the gap. The program built a middle class, but its doors were mostly open to white veterans only.
Remember: a program can lift millions and still leave others behind, and both facts belong in the story.
